name: Crisis Management
description: Disaster management in Iran encompasses risk reduction, preparedness, emergency response, and recovery. National policy documents connect these tasks, while the assessment of the 2019 floods illustrates the practical challenge of coordinating reconstruction across sectors and places.

seo.title: Crisis Management in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's disaster-management framework, the relationship between prevention and recovery, and the limits of available implementation evidence.

content.heading: More than emergency response
content.content:
In this context, crisis management means managing disasters rather than resolving political disputes. Iran's National Disaster Management Strategy covers prediction, prevention, risk reduction, preparedness, response, reconstruction, and rehabilitation. Its scope therefore extends beyond the dramatic period when rescue teams reach an affected neighborhood: it also concerns decisions made before an event and the conditions under which communities rebuild afterward. [s1]

These distinctions matter when reading institutional announcements. Publishing a strategy establishes an intended framework; it does not by itself demonstrate that buildings have become safer, warnings reach everyone, or essential services can continue during disruption. The strategy's public description is evidence of policy scope, rather than an independent evaluation of operational effectiveness. [s1]

content.heading: Connecting national and provincial planning
content.content:
A United Nations account published in January 2020 describes the planning documents required under the new disaster-management law. They include a national strategy, national and provincial risk-reduction plans, national and provincial preparedness-and-response plans, and a national reconstruction-and-rehabilitation plan. This structure separates preparation for an emergency from the longer task of restoring communities afterward. [s2]

The same account says that the National Disaster Management Organization assigned responsibility for the supplementary-document exercise to the Natural Disaster Research Institute, affiliated with the Housing Foundation. UN-Habitat, the United Nations agency concerned with settlements and urban development, had been requested to lead preparation of the national reconstruction-and-rehabilitation plan. These are documented assignments at that time, not confirmation that every resulting plan was completed or implemented. [s2]

content.heading: What the flood assessment demonstrates
content.content:
The post-disaster needs assessment following Iran's 2019 floods provides a concrete example of recovery planning. The government-led exercise examined three pilot provinces with United Nations technical support. It brought together information from ministries, provincial and local authorities, and field surveys to assess effects and identify recovery needs. Its geographic scope must be preserved: findings for the pilot provinces are not automatically national totals. [s3]

The report distinguishes damage to assets from wider losses and recovery requirements. For an urban reader, this is a useful way to understand why replacing a damaged structure and restoring a functioning service are related but different tasks. The assessment also argues for incorporating resilience into recovery, so reconstruction reduces vulnerability to future disasters rather than simply replacing what existed. [s3]

content.title: Distinct components of the documented planning framework
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Disaster-management planning framework"] -->|"Includes"| B["National strategy"]
  A -->|"Includes"| C["National and provincial risk-reduction plans"]
  A -->|"Includes"| D["National and provincial preparedness and response plans"]
  A -->|"Includes"| E["National reconstruction and rehabilitation plan"]
```
content.summary: The arrows identify categories of planning documents reported by the United Nations in January 2020. They do not represent operational command, funding, or proof of implementation.

name: Street Lighting
description: Street lighting connects urban public space with electricity infrastructure and equipment maintenance. Iranian energy documentation records earlier LED retrofit pilots, while industry sources illustrate the distinction between roadway lighting and broader decorative illumination.

seo.title: Street Lighting in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the evidence for Iran's street-lighting modernization, the difference between pilots and widespread adoption, and remaining research gaps.

content.heading: Different lights, different functions
content.content:
Urban lighting is a broader subject than the lamps lining a road. Iran Omid, an Iranian lighting supplier, describes work involving roadways, parks, squares, recreational areas, and decorative installations, with municipal, public, and private clients. Its account illustrates the range of applications within the domestic lighting industry. It should not be read as an inventory of public assets or an independent assessment of their condition. [s1]

This distinction helps clarify the subject of street lighting. A roadway installation, a park-lighting scheme, and illumination intended to emphasize a building's appearance may sit within the same commercial sector, but evidence about one does not establish the quality or coverage of the others. The supplier's portfolio description supports this distinction in applications; it does not establish a nationwide division of maintenance responsibilities. [s1]

content.heading: Evidence of earlier modernization
content.content:
Iran's energy balance for Solar Hijri year 1393 documents pilot work replacing street-lighting equipment with LED technology in several electricity-distribution areas, including Golestan, Yazd, South Khorasan, and Isfahan city. The report places these activities within an electricity-efficiency program. This provides historical evidence that LED modernization was already being tested through distribution-company projects, rather than evidence of a recent nationwide conversion. [s2]

The reporting calendar matters. A Solar Hijri reporting year must retain its original label unless its Gregorian boundaries are established. Equally, pilot results cannot be expanded into national savings without knowing the number and type of installations, operating conditions, and measurement method. The inspected material does not provide a comparable annual series from which to reconstruct adoption across Iranian cities. [s2]

content.heading: How to read upgrade claims
content.content:
The domestic industry's description of LED products emphasizes alternatives to older metal-halide and high-pressure-sodium light sources. This establishes the technology being offered, while leaving the performance of a particular public installation to be demonstrated separately. A manufacturer's account is useful evidence about its products and stated activities; it cannot establish citywide energy savings or independently verify public-service outcomes. [s1]

For this page, the strongest defensible conclusion is therefore limited: official historical reporting documents retrofit pilots, and a supplier's account shows the range of urban applications served by the lighting industry. A fuller account needs current utility and municipal records that distinguish installed equipment from proposed replacements, and measured results from expected benefits. The available evidence does not support a claim that modernization is complete or uniform across Iran. [s1][s2]

name: Citizen Service Systems
description: Citizen service systems provide channels for communicating municipal requests, complaints, and suggestions. Historical documentation from Tehran shows efforts to connect message registration, follow-up, feedback, and public reporting, while leaving current implementation and performance unresolved.

seo.title: Citizen Service Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Tehran's documented municipal feedback initiatives and why registering a request differs from verifying its resolution.

content.heading: From receiving messages to following them through
content.content:
A historical account published on Tehran council member Bahareh Arvin's website describes proposed improvements to the municipal systems known as 137 and 1888 within Tehran Man, the municipality's website and application. The account concerns a committee meeting in 2020; it is evidence of the work being discussed then, rather than a current service directory. [s1]

The proposals addressed registration, follow-up, and feedback. They also included publishing thematic maps and message information. Read together, these proposals reveal an important distinction in service design: receiving a resident's message is only one part of the process. Tracking how it is handled and reporting the result require additional functions. [s1]

content.heading: An improvement agenda is not proof of delivery
content.content:
The meeting account proposed feedback during handling and at completion. It also discussed an application programming interface, a software connection intended to let other urban-service developers use registration and tracking functions. These were proposed actions, not demonstrated operating capabilities. The inspected account does not establish their completion, current availability, or effect on resolution times. [s1]

A reliable contemporary guide therefore needs more than historical descriptions of digital features. This page remains a documented introduction pending verification of current channels, eligibility requirements, accessibility, and independently supported service outcomes.
